claims.text: Brittle behavior in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys emerges from stress- and temperature-induced grain-boundary chemical ordering or nanosegregation.
Brittle behavior does not emerge from conventional intermetallic precipitation in the proposed HEA.
Grain-boundary chemical ordering or nanosegregation reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Pre-aging can modify the initial grain-boundary chemistry and thereby distinguish the proposed mechanism.
The initial material is a single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy.
The as-cast material has homogeneous grain-boundary composition.
The controlled intervention is pre-aging followed by mechanical testing across strain rate and temperature.
Embrittlement is observed at intermediate temperatures and high strain rates.
Applied stress in specific temperature regimes induces chemical segregation and local ordering at HEA grain boundaries.
The stress-induced local compositional change undermines intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion causes a transition from ductile to brittle failure.
Conventional-alloy brittle behavior is linked to grain-boundary precipitation.
Samples with intentionally altered grain-boundary chemistry will show a measurable shift in the onset threshold for brittle behavior relative to as-cast samples.
The altered samples will show detectable changes in local grain-boundary chemical ordering.
The as-cast baseline has a specific threshold for brittle behavior under standard loading conditions.
The proposed effects occur within service-relevant intermediate and high temperatures and engineering-relevant strain rates.
Conditions outside the specified service regimes may not produce the predicted grain-boundary ordering.
Threshold conditions and toughness changes may vary with alloy composition and processing history.
The proposed controlled comparison uses standard as-cast samples and pre-aged samples tested under identical strain-rate and temperature conditions.
